Justice GK Ilanthiraiyan quashed the First Information Report (FIR) against one Chandirasekar, on finding that there was no material to show that he had cast the vote attributed to him in Chennai’s Virugambakkam Assembly constituency. items.title: Tried to softly bend laws to ensure justice: Chief Justice DK Upadhyaya bids farewell to Delhi High Court
items.summary: Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya on Tuesday bid farewell to the Delhi High Court, following his recent elevation as a judge of the Supreme Court. Speaking at the full-court farewell reference organised in his honour at the Delhi High Court, Chief Justice (CJ) Upadhyaya underscored that the Chief Justice is merely the “first among equals." CJ Upadhyaya described judging as an effort to bind law, justice, and compassion together. He shared insights into his judicial journey, his approach to justice, and his experience as the Chief Justice of the Delhi High Court. "Like other judges, I came across situations when the law was not able to ensure a just outcome and appeared isolated from justice. In such situations, I tried to softly bend the law towards justice for the deserving litigants. To be able to do so has been a blessing," he said. Reflecting on the debate between "good versus great judges," he went on to remark, "My endeavour has been to be a good judge, may not be a great judge." items.title: Law clerk experience cannot be equated with bench clerk's for judicial service eligibility: Supreme Court
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday observed that the experience gained by a law clerk cannot be equated with that of a bench clerk for the purpose of fulfilling the eligibility requirement of prior legal practice to take the judicial service examinations [ Tapasmita Sutar vs Union of India ]. A law clerk is a law graduate engaged for a fixed term to help a judge with research and drafting, while a bench clerk is a court staff member who manages courtroom administration, such as calling cases, handling files and recording orders dictated by a judge. A Bench comprising Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant , Justice Joymalya Bagchi , and Justice V Mohana today observed that the two roles cannot be equated while determining a person's eligibility to take the judicial services exam. CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, Justice V Mohana The Court was hearing a petition moved by a judicial services aspirant who had served as a bench clerk in the district judiciary. items.title: 3 new Supreme Court judges take oath; strength of court rises to 37
items.summary: Three new judges for the Supreme Court of India were administered the oath of office on Tuesday afternoon. The newly appointed judges are Justice Sunita Agarwal (formerly Chief Justice of the Gujarat High Court), Justice DK Upadhyay (formerly Chief Justice of the Delhi High Court) and Justice Aparesh Kumar Singh (formerly Chief Justice of the Telangana High Court). Justice Sunita Agarwal, Justice DK Upadhyaya, Justice Aparesh Kumar Singh The Central government had notified their appointments as Supreme Court judges on Monday, following a recommendation made by a Supreme Court Collegium on September 28. With their appointments, the top court now has a working strength of 37 judges, just one short of its sanctioned strength of 38 judges. Justice Agarwal, who is originally a judge of the Allahabad High Court, has been the Chief Justice of the Gujarat High Court since July 2023. She graduated in law from Awadh University in 1989 and has been in the legal profession since December 1990. She was appointed as a judge in November 2011. items.title: Police must create fear in minds of goons: Supreme Court in suo motu case on women's safety
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday urged the Delhi Police not to hesitate in taking strict action against 'goons' found threatening the safety of women in Delhi, and to instil genuine fear in the minds of those who intend to commit crimes against women. A Bench of Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran underscored that policing cannot remain confined to files and orders on paper, but must translate into visible deterrence on the streets. "We are in a country like India. Merely putting things on paper is not enough. You need to get into action. If you have to be a little more strict, a little more harsh, do not hesitate. There will be people who will raise a hue and cry about Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty), but you have to do your duty," the Bench observed orally. The Court noted that the goal must be crime prevention rather than action after the crime has occurred. "There should be a fear, a fright in the mind of the man who is prone to commit such offences. Unless that fear and fright is created ki ‘ab kuch kiya toh marr jayenge’ (if we do anything now, we will be finished), you will not be able to prevent such crimes.
